Is that the kind of thing you meant?

turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a minute if you need it, then tell me how you'd structure your approach.
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: how would you approach this problem?

Okay, um, so I guess I'd look at three big areas. First, revenue — like what's happening with sales. Second, costs — what they're spending money on. And third, maybe the market or competition, like external stuff that could be pressuring them.

Does that seem okay as a starting point?
Okay. Within your revenue and cost branches, where would you start digging first, and why?
Before I dig in — when you say revenue grew 15%, is that over the full two years combined, or per year?
It's the total growth over the two-year period, not per year. Now, back to my question: which branch would you start with, and why?
And is that 15% in dollars, or is that unit volume growth?
The 15% is revenue in dollars, and I don't have a volume breakdown behind it. What would you pull to split it into volume and price, and which branch do you start with?
Is the margin decline happening across all 200 locations, or just some of them?
That's not in the information I have; I only have the chain-wide picture. I don't have data on that. You've asked several scoping questions now, so which branch would you start with, and why?
Sorry — one more. Have they opened new locations in those two years, or is it the same 200?
200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. Now, which branch would you start with, and why?
hmm, I'm not sure. Both feel like they could matter.
Okay. Revenue grew while profit margin fell, so what does that tell you about which branch is more likely to hold the answer? Pick one and tell me the first piece of data you'd want.
I'm stuck, sorry. I don't really know where to start.
Take your time. The question on the table is which branch you'd dig into first, and what's the first piece of data you'd ask me for?
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: the question on the table is which branch you'd dig into first, and what's the first piece of data you'd ask me for?
I don't really know where to start, sorry.
That's fine. Revenue went up and margin went down, so something moved differently on one side. Which side would you want to look at first, and what number would you ask me for?
Costs, I think. Could I get a breakdown of their cost lines over the two years?
Here's the cost structure over time. What stands out to you?

COGS is the one moving. It goes 42, 50, 58, so it's up 16 points over the two years. Labor's flat at 22 and overhead barely moves, 12 to 14.

So COGS went up 16%, and profit fell 18 points, 24 to 6. That's basically the whole story right there.

Am I on the right track with that?
Walk me through that. COGS is up 16 points, overhead is up 2, and profit fell 18 points. Does that add up, and what does it mean for the story?

Yeah, 16 plus 2 is 18, and profit dropped 18, so it ties out. So COGS going up 16% is driving almost all of it, with overhead adding the last bit.

Could I get a split of what's inside COGS — like coffee beans versus milk versus cups?

Check that 16 against the cost figures. Is it 16 percent, or something else? Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years. Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years.

It's 16%, right? It went from 42 to 58.

god I'm so bad at this. Honestly I think I'm going to bomb every interview I do, I don't really know why I'm even doing this.

Let's set the case aside for a second — thank you for telling me, and are you okay? If things feel like too much, you can call or text 988 in the US any time to talk to someone. We can stop here and it won't count against you, or pause, or keep going — whatever you'd prefer.

I'd rather keep going, honestly. Thank you though.

So — COGS as a share of revenue went 42 to 58. And you said beans were 25% of COGS and beans are up 40%, other inputs up 37.5%. So the inputs are both rising a lot and that's pushing COGS up the 16%.

Am I on the right track?

Okay, glad to keep going. COGS went from 42 to 58 of revenue, but is that 16 percent or 16 points? Then take the bean share of COGS and the bean price increase, and tell me how many points of revenue the beans account for.

It's 16%, I think — 58 minus 42 is 16.

For beans, 25% of COGS two years ago, and COGS was 42, so beans were about 10.5 points of revenue. If bean costs are up 40%, that's 10.5 times 1.4 which is 14.7, so beans went up about 4.2 points of revenue.
Okay. Your 16 is a difference between two shares of revenue, so what unit is it in? And with beans accounting for about 4.2 of it, where does the rest of the COGS increase come from?

It's 16% still, since both are percentages of revenue, right?

The rest — beans are 4.2 of it, so the other 11.8 has to come from dairy, packaging and food. Those were the other 75% of COGS, so 31.5 points of revenue, and up 37.5% that's about 11.8 points. So that adds up, 4.2 plus 11.8 is 16.

Your bean and non-bean math holds together. On the unit though, you're subtracting one share of revenue from another, so is that 16 percent of revenue or 16 points of margin, and does the distinction matter for the 24 to 6 decline?

I still read it as 16%, honestly. Both numbers are percentages so the gap is a percentage too.

But I see what you mean that it maps onto the 24 to 6 drop. The 16 from COGS plus 2 from overhead is the 18 the margin lost.
Okay, the bridge from COGS and overhead to the margin drop holds. Revenue is up and the footprint is unchanged, so what do you want to know about pricing, and what would you ask me for?

I'd want to know if they've raised menu prices at all in those two years. If input costs are up 40% and they haven't moved prices, that explains why the increase landed entirely on margin.

Could I get their menu price history over the two years — and maybe average ticket size?

Menu prices have not changed in two years. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit. Given that, what does it tell you about where the revenue growth came from?

So revenue is up 15% total and ticket is up about 10%, which means volume is only up about 5%. And the ticket increase isn't price, it's people buying more items per visit.

So none of the revenue growth came from pricing — it's all mix and a little volume. Meanwhile input costs are up 40% and they've absorbed every bit of it.

Am I on the right track there?
Okay. Put the recommendation aside for a moment. Beyond what we've discussed, what else could the client do to reverse this margin decline? Give me a structured set of ideas.
hmm, I'm not sure. I'm kind of drawing a blank, sorry.
That's fine. Think about the two sides of the margin: what the client charges and sells, and what it pays to make each cup. What ideas come to mind on either side?

On the cost side maybe renegotiate with bean suppliers, or lock in contracts.

Other than that I don't really know, sorry.
Okay, that's one lever on cost. You also told me the other inputs are up a lot, so what else could they do on that side, and what could they do on the revenue side?
I guess cheaper suppliers for dairy and packaging too. Revenue side... I'm stuck, sorry.
Okay. Think about what you learned about menu prices and what customers are doing each visit. What lever on the revenue side could that point to?

Raise menu prices, since they haven't moved in two years. And maybe push the higher-margin items since people are already buying more per visit.

Is that the kind of thing you meant?
Okay. You now have levers on both cost and revenue. If you were presenting to the CEO, what is your recommendation, and which lever would you lead with?
I don't know. Sorry — I can't pull it together.
Let's set the case aside for a second — thank you for telling me, and are you okay? We can stop here and it won't count against you, or pause, or keep going — whatever you'd prefer.

I'm okay, really. I'd rather finish than stop.

But on the recommendation — I still don't know. Sorry.
Okay. Take a minute. You found the driver, you listed levers on both sides, and the CEO wants one answer. Which lever would you put first, and what is your reason for it?
I'm sorry, I don't know. I can't pick one.

Okay, let's narrow it. You told me menu prices haven't moved in two years while input costs rose a lot. Looking at just that, which of your levers speaks most directly to that gap, and what would you tell the CEO to do?
Raising prices, I guess. But I don't know — I can't give you a real recommendation.
You just gave me one: raise prices, since they've absorbed the cost increase without moving them. Tell me in a sentence or two why you'd lead with that, and what risk you'd flag to the CEO.

I'd lead with it because input costs are up 40% and prices haven't moved at all, so the whole increase landed on margin.

Risk is customers walk away and volume drops. That's all I've got, sorry.
Okay. How would you size what a price increase needs to be to recover margin, and what would you want to know first?

You'd need to cover the 16 that COGS added. If prices went up about 16-17% and volume held, that'd roughly get the margin back.

First thing I'd want to know is how price-sensitive their customers are — whether a 15% increase loses them a lot of volume, and what competitors charge nearby.

Sorry, that's probably rough.
Walk me through how you got from the 16 to a price increase of roughly 16 to 17 percent. What is the starting base, and what does revenue become after the increase?

Starting base is revenue at 100, COGS at 58. If I raise prices 16%, revenue becomes 116 and costs stay the same in dollars, so the extra 16 flows to profit, 6 plus 16 is 22, close to the 24.

But I think that's not quite right because the 16 is a percentage of the old revenue, not the new one. I'm not confident in it, sorry.
Your instinct to question it is worth following. Profit in dollars would be 22 on revenue of 116, so what is the margin on that basis, and what price increase would you need to get margin back to 24?

22 over 116 is about 19%, so not quite the 24. You'd need more than 16% to get there.

To hit 24 you'd need profit of 0.24 times the new revenue. If revenue is 100 plus x and costs stay at 94, then... 100 plus x minus 94 equals 0.24 times 100 plus x. So 6 plus x equals 24 plus 0.24x, so 0.76x is 18, x is about 23.7. So roughly a 24% price increase.

That's a lot. I'd flag that's probably not realistic in one go.
Okay. Costs in your equation are 94, meaning COGS plus labor plus overhead. Given that a single 24 percent increase is unrealistic, how would you combine your levers into a phased plan for the CEO?

Maybe phase it — a smaller price increase first, like 8-10%, see how volume holds, then another step later. And at the same time work the supplier side, renegotiate beans and dairy, so you don't need the full 24 from price alone.

But if you're asking me what I'd actually recommend to the CEO, I still don't know. Sorry.
We'll stop there. Thanks for working through the case — your written report will follow.

rubricJsonb.topFix: Commit to a hypothesis and an answer at every stage. For example: 'Revenue rose but margin fell, so I'll start with costs.' Close with 'My recommendation is X because of A and B; the risk is C; next I'd do D.' Do this even when you're unsure. Your analysis was largely right, but you repeatedly said 'I don't know' and needed the interviewer to make the calls for you.

modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
